newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- $8.0 billion in TIPS.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- $8.0 billion in TIPS.

text.p: With the cupboard almost bare of new economic data, the main feature of U.S. government securities trading on Wednesday is likely to be the Treasury's sale of $8.0 billion in five-year Treasury Inflation Protected Securities (TIPS), analysts said.

The government reports U.S. wholesale inventory levels for May at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. Economists Reuters polled estimated that wholesale inventories rose 0.2 percent in May after falling 0.7 percent in April. Those data are unlikely to have more than the slightest impact on the market, analysts said.
"The market will probably tend to focus on the TIPs auction," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities Inc.
Flanagan said the market is trying to find out what the constituency is for inflation-protected securities when the fear of inflation is fading.

"If there's little or no inflation, why do you need something that's indexed to inflation?" said Flanagan. "That could work against the reception for the TIPS or at least stem some enthusiasm for them. This is an environment in which you're actually hearing some chatter about deflation."
Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said the market would not trade higher or lower based on what happens with the TIPS auction.
With the calendar nearly devoid of new economic data, the TIPS auction could be the main feature of the session.
"But individuals won't view the relative success or failure of the TIPS auction as an indication of the way nominal yields will go," he said.
Alexy and Larry Dyer, bond market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, noted that the (TIPS) had actually traded counter to the overall market over the last couple of months.

"In some ways that makes sense because you buy them for inflation protection and when there's no inflation, people ask, 'How much do I want to pay for that protection?'" said Alexy. "On the other hand, they're cheap compared to some other forms of safety nets and they've gotten cheaper."
The when-issued yield on the five-year TIPS scheduled for sale on Wednesday was 3.6475 percent late Tuesday, up more than 10 basis points from Monday.
Yields on 10-year TIPS rose to 3.685 percent from 3.61 percent on Monday. They were originally sold with a yield of 3.449 percent.
"TIPS have always been a technical issue, not a mainstream security," said Dyer. "TIPS have underperformed."
Dyer said yields could go even higher as the bidding deadline for the auction nears on Wednesday.

And some players might be interested in swapping 10-year TIPS for the five-year TIPS. Managers holding five-year corporate inflation-protected bonds might find the five-year TIPS "a more natural hedge" for their positions since the biggest portion of corporate swap deals done involved five-year maturities.
Also, some people who have been looking at the TIPS product might find the five-year easier to buy than the 10-year because it's less risky, Dyer said.
"And because the TIPs have cheapened up quite a bit, the Street could buy them at a level that they now feel represents value," Dyer said.
The benchmark 30-year issue ended at 100-15/32 on Tuesday, down 5/32 to yield 6.59 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Wednesday.
